query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multiscale simulation method that couples on‐the-fly machine‐learned interatomic potentials for phonon dynamics with concurrent first‐principles electronic structure calculations can explicitly decouple and separately predict the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities in HfNbTaTiZr, achieving a 20–30% reduction in prediction error relative to traditional Debye or DFT-elastic constant based approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr prepared in two forms: nearly defect‐free crystals and crystals doped with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Apply a coupled simulation approach that uses machine-learned force fields to capture realistic phonon lifetime distributions and concurrently utilizes DFT-based calculations to determine temperature-dependent electron scattering rates.
generation.conditions: Simulations and subsequent experimental validations conducted over two temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (<200 K), where lattice and electronic contributions are expected to be comparable, and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) corresponding to conditions observed in oxygen-doped samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Intrinsic chemical disorder and associated lattice distortions that modify local interatomic force constants and electron scattering pathways, further influenced by the presence of oxygen impurities.
generation.mechanism: By using machine learning to dynamically train interatomic potentials on atomic-scale simulation data, the method accurately resolves phonon propagation and lifetime. Simultaneously, first-principles electronic structure calculations capture temperature-dependent electron scattering rates, enabling the decoupling of lattice and electronic heat transport phenomena without relying on oversimplified parameters such as a single Debye temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach predicts that, below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal conductivities will be nearly equal, while in oxygen-doped samples at high temperatures (300–1200 K), the total thermal conductivity will fall in the 10–17 W/(K m) range. Overall, predictions should be about 20–30% more accurate than those from traditional models that conflate the two transport channels.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and computational methods based on modified Debye temperature estimates or DFT-derived elastic properties applied to idealized, defect-free bulk crystals.
generation.boundary: The model is applicable only for bulk HfNbTaTiZr under controlled defect conditions (including up to ~1 wt.% oxygen) and within the specified temperature ranges (<200 K and 300–1200 K). Its performance outside this compositional and temperature window remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage improvement and the model’s applicability beyond the defined boundary conditions remain uncertain until validated by targeted experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct detailed experiments on both defect-free and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr samples across the low (<200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes. Simultaneously, perform simulations with the multiscale method to predict separate lattice and electronic contributions. Use experimental techniques such as refined Wiedemann-Franz analysis (to extract electronic contributions from electrical resistivity measurements) and phonon spectroscopy (to deduce lattice contributions).
measurements: Total thermal conductivity (κ_total) over the temperature range
Separated electronic (κ_e) and lattice (κ_l) thermal conductivities using independent measurement techniques
Temperature-dependent trends confirming near-equal contributions at low temperatures and matching overall conductivity (10–17 W/(K m)) at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the individually predicted values for κ_e and κ_l deviate by more than ±30% from the experimentally determined values, or if the expected parity between lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The entropy of an HEA encompasses contributions that extend beyond the straightforward entropy of mixing, including vibrational, electronic, and magnetic components (). We note that due to the differing atomic sizes of individual alloy components, the atoms in an HEA do not sit on ideal lattice sites (defined by the Bravais lattice and basis vectors). Hence, the variation in atomic size and deviation of atom locations from the ideal lattice in a random solid solution provides an additional contribution to the entropy, which we denote noncomposition entropy ΔSnc. (This noncomposition entropy is distinct from the entropy of mixing ΔSm.) In a single-component glassy system, ΔSnc is referred to as “configurational” or “information” entropy or “complexity” (). Random local lattice distortions (misfit) are responsible, in part, for the high strength of high entropy alloys (e.g. see Refs ()). Here, we focus on the thermodynamic implications of such random distortions. The effects of atomic-size-induced distortions on structure and properties are difficult to assess in real alloy systems since these are necessarily convoluted with variations in bonding between different types of atoms ().

decision.trend: Early work first tried to capture thermal transport in high‐entropy alloys by modifying simple parameters – for example, by adjusting atomic masses and force constants (often via Debye‐like approximations) or by estimating elastic properties from DFT and then coupling them to analytical conductivity formulas. Later studies moved toward explicitly resolving phonon dynamics in disordered systems and even began combining on‐the‐fly machine learning with first‐principles calculations to capture lattice dynamics and thermoelectric behavior. In particular, work on phonon propagation in HEAs (PMC9726824) and subsequent machine learning–aided DFT investigations (PMC9822225) addressed the inherent complexity of disordered vibrational modes, though they still did not separate the lattice contribution from the electronic one. More recent work on refractory HEAs (PMC11136967) has begun to address electrical transport using low‐frequency conductivity models but leaves the coupling issue unresolved.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, no approach to date has unambiguously decoupled lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr across the low-temperature regime (where contributions are comparable) and the high-temperature regime (as evidenced by 10–17 W/(K m) total conductivity in oxygen‐doped samples). The main unsolved challenge remains how to predict independently and accurately the complex lattice (phononic) and electronic scattering processes in realistic, defect‐inclusive models of these alloys without relying on overly simplified parameters like a single Debye temperature.
decision.lever: Developing a multiscale simulation approach that couples machine-learned interatomic potentials with electronic structure calculations to separately extract phonon lifetime distributions and electron scattering rates
decision.why: This approach directly follows the progression from simplistic Debye or DFT-elastic based models toward more refined, on-the-fly machine learning methods. By explicitly decoupling the two heat carriers in a realistic, chemically disordered HfNbTaTiZr model – including both defect-free and oxygen-doped networks – the method can predict lattice and electronic contributions separately. The hypothesis would be testable by quantifying an expected reduction in prediction error (e.g., a 20–30% improvement relative to current analytical estimates) over the distinct temperature regimes (<200 K and 300–1200 K) and would be falsified if decisive comparisons with low-temperature (comparable lattice and electron contributions) or high-temperature (total conductivity within 10–17 W/(K m)) measurements show significant deviations from the predicted separated contributions.
